title: Spelling mistakes in DNA
hook: Change one letter of a gene. Does the protein change?

knows: DNA is written in four letters
doesNotKnow: that many single-letter changes leave the protein unchanged
that the slack sits mostly in the third letter of a codon

misconception: Any change in the code changes the protein.
objective: The learner can explain that the genetic code is redundant: of the 549 single-letter changes to amino-acid codons, 134 (24%) keep the same amino acid, almost all at the third letter.

claims.text: In the standard genetic code, three-letter codons name amino acids, and several codons can name the same amino acid.
claims.source: Standard genetic code table (Nirenberg & Matthaei 1961; Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, ch. 6).

claims.text: The 61 amino-acid codons have 549 single-letter changes; 134 (24%) keep the amino acid, 392 give a different amino acid and 23 give a stop.
claims.source: Enumerated from the standard code table in Demo.tsx; artifacts/scratch/w5life/codons.mjs gives total 549, same 134, new 392, stop 23, 24.4%.

claims.text: By position, the same amino acid is kept by 8 of 183 first-letter changes, 0 of 183 second-letter changes and 126 of 183 third-letter changes.
claims.source: Same enumeration (codons.mjs, pos array: 8, 0, 126 of 183 each).

claims.text: For the three codons on the stage: CTT (Leu) keeps Leu for all 3 third-letter changes; TAT (Tyr) keeps Tyr for 1 change (TAC) and gives stop for 2 (TAA, TAG); GGA (Gly) keeps Gly for all 3 third-letter changes and gives a stop for TGA.
claims.source: Standard code table; codons.mjs lists the nine changes of each. The codon is a model of the code, not of any particular gene; DNA letters are shown on the coding strand.

recall.question: Roughly what share of single-letter changes to a codon leave its amino acid unchanged, and which letter is most often silent?
options: About a quarter, the third letter
About three quarters, the first letter
recall.why: The standard code has built-in slack: about 24% of changes are silent, nearly all at the third letter of the codon.
